newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Economic theorists win Nobel prize for human touch.
newsitem.headline: Economic theorists win Nobel prize for human touch.

text.p: Two financial gurus were awarded the 1996 Nobel Prize for Economics on Tuesday for adding human nature into the formulation of tax policies and other financial decision making.

British professor James Mirrlees, 60, of Cambridge University, and Canadian William Vickrey, 82, won the prize for "contribution to the economic theory of incentives under asymmetric information" for research spread over 20 years.

Between them Vickrey and Mirrlees focused on how governments, companies or any organisation could cope with constantly lacking complete information - or asymmetric information - but still make strategic decisions.
The two economists, who are not widely known in the economic world, have never met even though jointly their work has sowed the seeds of a new branch in economic theory.

"The importance of this prize is that the methodology can be applied in all kinds of contracts," Karl-Gustaf Lofgren, member of the Nobel economic prize committee, told Reuters, after the award was announced in Stockholm.
"This methodology has spread into textbooks of micro-economic theory. It is not very often you get new chapters in text books."

The Nobel economics prize, which is one of six annual Nobel awards, was founded in 1968 to commemorate the 300 year jubilee of Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, and is awarded by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.

Jorgen Weibull, Nobel economics committee member, said the area of Vickrey and Mirrlees' research, was a key area for economists, factoring incentive, capability and social responsibility into the economic equation.
"Much of economic theory now centres on imperfect competition," Weibull told a press conference. "A lot of work is going on right now on extensions to this work."
Vickrey, in the 1940s, produced research on different types of auctions and a design for maximum economic efficiency.
But he also became known for his work on income taxation, rewriting the 19th Century philosophy that all differences in income should be neutralised by taxation.
Vickrey said progressive taxation affected individuals' incentive to work and he reformulated the problem so that individuals' productivity should not be penalised by tax.

The Canadian-born economist, who is now Professor Emeritus at Columbia University, New York, was unavailable for comment immediately after the $1.12 million award was announced but planned to hold a press conference later in the day.

Some 25 years later, Mirrlees built on Vickrey's work, mastering the mathematical complications of Vickrey's work, drastically simplifying the issue and applying it to many other areas of economic theory.
He tried to find the optimum tax level by researching links between levels of taxation and people's incentive to work.
Mirrlees told Reuters that the most exciting moment of his life came "when I finally cracked the optimal tax problem".
"It came in a flash and it was very satisfactory. That was in 1968," he told Reuters.
"It was really exciting to solve a problem, a bit embarrassing to get a prize."
Mirrlees, who was born in Minnigaff, Scotland, is now teaching economics at the University of Cambridge, England.
The Nobel Economic Prize was the third Nobel this year.
The literature prize was awarded last Thursday to Polish poet Wislawa Szymborska while Australian Peter Doherty and Swiss Rolf Zinkernagel won the medicine prize on Monday.
The winners of the physics and chemistry awards will be announced in Stockholm on Wednesday and the Nobel Peace Prize will be awarded in Oslo on Friday.
